run.brief: You own exactly /Users/deepfates/Hacking/github/deepfates/dspy_elixir/identity/inbox/14-research-epistemic.json. You are not alone in the codebase: edit only that path; do not revert, stage, commit, or format anything else. Read identity/README.md, identity/atlas.json, identity/schema/portfolio.schema.json, README.md, docs/DSEX_PHILOSOPHY.md, and one current valid portfolio such as identity/inbox/09-boundaries-limits-care.json. Create one valid schema_version 1 portfolio with run id run-14-research-epistemic, atlas_version 1, ISO UTC generated_at, method and generator name "epistemic research adversary", generator kind agent/provider openai/model gpt-5.6-sol/reasoning_effort xhigh/agent_id null. Put this full brief verbatim in run.brief. intended_territories: mathematics-logic, science-experiment, measurement-evidence, uncertainty-probability, feedback-control. intended_strategies: technical-borrowing, descriptive-category, proper-mythic-historical, institutional-community, acronym-initialism. intended_audiences: pl-researchers, dspy-gepa-researchers, ml-researchers, eval-research-ops, applied-lm-engineers. Generate exactly 100 candidate observations with contiguous ordinals 1..100 and exactly 20 wildcard true. Do not rank, filter, deduplicate, browse, availability-check, or suppress odd/bad/colliding candidates. Use only valid atlas IDs. Explore names a technically skeptical research audience could discuss in a paper, benchmark, lab meeting, citation, package import, and critical review. Range across empirical method, optimization and search, programs and transformations, uncertainty, measurement, ablation, feedback, epistemic humility, institutions, historical figures, acronyms, and intentional category errors. Explicitly surface where a term falsely suggests theoremhood, convergence, static typing, causal identification, objective metrics, autonomous discovery, or parity with DSPy/GEPA. Respect the product boundary: a pre-release Elixir/OTP library for declared, callable, measurable, improvable LM programs, with a credible typed textual/artifact optimization horizon; not an official DSPy port, static proof system, universal agent OS, provider SDK, or guaranteed autonomous self-improvement engine. Every observation needs substantive rationale, honest etymology when applicable, semantic territories and lexical strategies, architecture lenses, audiences, and concerns. Validate with jq and report only after the file is complete.

candidates.rationale: Frames the library as a way to make LM program behavior inspectable through trials, datasets, and recorded outcomes. It is plain enough for a paper title or lab discussion while leaving the Elixir implementation to the descriptor.
candidates.etymology: Empirical derives through Latin empiricus from Greek empeirikos, meaning experienced; program derives from Greek programma, a written public notice.
known_concerns: The phrase can imply that every program is supported by a sound experimental design, even when its metric, sample, and comparison are weak.

candidates.rationale: Joins experimental trials to durable records of candidates, scores, and optimizer lineage. The name supports critical review because it points toward evidence retention rather than a magical improvement claim.
candidates.etymology: Trial comes from Anglo-French trier, to test or sift; ledger is an English bookkeeping term for an organized record.
known_concerns: Ledger language may suggest tamper-proof provenance or financial accounting that ordinary persisted optimizer reports do not provide.

candidates.rationale: Uses the research demand for repeatable results as both a noun-like identity and a command-shaped package name. It would keep reproducibility in view when discussing stochastic LM evaluations and saved program variants.
candidates.etymology: From Latin replicare, to fold back or repeat; its modern scientific sense concerns repeating a study or result.
known_concerns: The imperative can promise reproducibility despite provider drift, stochastic sampling, hidden model changes, and incomplete experimental metadata.

candidates.rationale: Centers attempts to disconfirm claims about an LM program instead of only searching for a higher score. In a review or benchmark, it would invite attention to counterexamples, regressions, and adverse test cases.
candidates.etymology: Built from falsify, ultimately Latin falsus, false; in philosophy of science, falsification is strongly associated with Karl Popper.
known_concerns: It overstates what finite evaluations can refute and may imply a simple Popperian account of confirmation that does not fit statistical model behavior.

candidates.rationale: Imports the comparison group of experimental design into program optimization, emphasizing baselines and unchanged variants. Its deliberate institutional plural makes the identity sound more like a research collective than a generic AI product.
candidates.etymology: Control entered experimental vocabulary for conditions held fixed or used as a comparison; group derives through French from Italian gruppo.
known_concerns: LM program evaluations rarely support the clean isolation suggested by a controlled study, and 'control' also imports command-and-control connotations.

candidates.rationale: Names the data withheld from search and used to check whether an optimized artifact generalizes. The terse surface works in code and in a methodological critique of leakage between candidate generation and evaluation.
candidates.etymology: An English compound of hold and out; in statistics and machine learning it denotes data reserved from fitting or selection.
known_concerns: A holdout name can falsely reassure users that evaluation leakage, repeated peeking, and benchmark overfitting are automatically prevented.

candidates.rationale: Treats declared LM programs as artifacts placed under repeatable tests with replaceable models, metrics, and datasets. It is concrete enough for engineering use while retaining the experimental orientation of a lab bench.
candidates.etymology: Test comes through Old French from Latin testum, an earthen vessel used in assaying; bench is an Old English word for a long seat or work surface.
known_concerns: The mechanical metaphor can understate social and semantic validity questions and make benchmarks appear more objective than their construction permits.

candidates.rationale: Describes the operational cycle of call, measure, compare, revise, and call again. It keeps the feedback channel and its evidence visible without asserting that every loop improves the program.
candidates.etymology: Evidence comes from Latin evidentia, clarity or proof; loop is an English word for a closed curve, later used for repeated control flow.
known_concerns: Calling scores evidence may obscure construct validity, and loop language can imply autonomous continuous optimization rather than explicitly invoked bounded runs.

candidates.rationale: Makes disagreement between a measured score and the intended property the primary epistemic fact. As an intentionally uneasy brand, it would give critical reviewers a direct vocabulary for metric noise and misspecification.
candidates.etymology: Measurement derives from Latin mensura, measure; error derives from Latin errare, to wander or be mistaken.
known_concerns: The negative surface sounds like a defect report and could imply the library estimates formal error terms that its arbitrary user metrics may not define.

candidates.rationale: Names the question of whether an evaluation actually measures the capability or outcome it claims to measure. It is a deliberately academic category name that could discipline benchmark discussion around LM program optimization.
candidates.etymology: Construct is from Latin construere, to build together; validity is from Latin validus, strong, and became a technical term in measurement theory.
known_concerns: Using the term as a name could imply validated psychometric methodology or an objective metric guarantee that the library cannot supply.

candidates.rationale: Foregrounds disagreement among human or model judges instead of presenting one evaluator as ground truth. It could name a package concerned with storing structured feedback and comparing evaluation perspectives.
candidates.etymology: A modern technical compound: inter-, Latin for between, plus rater, one who assigns a rating.
known_concerns: It narrows the product to judge agreement and can suggest that agreement itself establishes correctness or fairness.

candidates.rationale: Borrows the statistical and metrological practice of aligning reported confidence or instrument output with observed frequencies. The term invites research scrutiny of uncertainty-bearing predictions and evaluator behavior.
candidates.etymology: From calibre, via French, for determining or adjusting scale; statistics uses calibration for correspondence between predicted probabilities and observed outcomes.
known_concerns: The library does not inherently produce calibrated probabilities, and the instrumentation metaphor can falsely imply traceable physical standards.

candidates.rationale: Uses the scientific notion of a measurable quantity and the systems notion of inspectable behavior. It fits traces, predictions, scores, and optimizer records while remaining compact as a module root.
candidates.etymology: From Latin observare, to watch or attend to; observable is a technical noun in physics and a descriptive term in software operations.
known_concerns: It collides conceptually with reactive programming and may suggest complete observability when provider internals and model reasoning remain inaccessible.

candidates.rationale: Connects evaluation instruments, tool-mediated action, and the pragmatic question of whether a program works for a declared purpose. In research prose it can carry both measurement and philosophy-of-science readings.
candidates.etymology: From Latin instrumentum, a tool or equipment; instrumentalism treats theories partly as tools for prediction rather than literal descriptions.
known_concerns: The philosophical term can reduce truth to utility, while the ordinary adjective is generic and may be mistaken for a provider tool SDK.

candidates.rationale: Turns benchmark judgment into an explicit institution with procedures, evidence, and appeal rather than a neutral scoreboard. The category error gives critics language for questioning who selects cases and legitimizes metrics.
candidates.etymology: Benchmark originally named a surveyor's mark on a bench-like support; court derives from Latin cohors through French for an enclosed place and judging body.
known_concerns: Judicial language imports authority, punishment, and due-process expectations while still risking benchmark reductionism and metric objectivity.

candidates.rationale: Names a bounded procedure for determining the composition or performance of a material, adapted here to program artifacts. Its compactness supports package imports and short benchmark names without promising a universal evaluation.
candidates.etymology: From Old French assai or essai, a trial or attempt; it shares ancestry with essay and became a technical term for analytical tests.
known_concerns: Materials-testing precision can overstate the validity and repeatability of language-model evaluations, and biomedical associations may mislead.

candidates.rationale: Emphasizes declared procedures for calling, evaluating, and revising LM programs across repeatable runs. It can function in a methods section and as an implementation identity for explicit runtime boundaries.
candidates.etymology: From Greek protokollon, the first sheet glued to a manuscript roll; it later came to mean an official procedure or communication convention.
known_concerns: Protocol can imply a stable interoperable standard or wire format, neither of which follows from a pre-release Elixir library.

candidates.rationale: Elevates failed improvements, ties, regressions, and inconclusive evaluations to first-class research outputs. It directly resists a portfolio narrative in which every optimizer run must demonstrate lift.
candidates.etymology: Negative derives from Latin negare, to deny; result derives from Latin resultare, to spring back, later meaning an outcome.
known_concerns: The surface has negative brand affect and may be misread as statistical proof of no effect rather than a noisy or underpowered observation.

candidates.rationale: Makes uncertainty around reported scores visible in the identity itself. The familiar graph element could anchor discussions of repeated runs, evaluator variance, and the limits of point estimates.
candidates.etymology: A modern statistical compound for a graphical mark that displays variability or uncertainty around an estimate.
known_concerns: Different error bars encode different quantities, and the name may imply valid inferential statistics even when samples are dependent or evaluator noise is unmodeled.

candidates.rationale: Connects runtime traces to claims about how a declared program behaved during a particular execution. It is useful in critical review because it distinguishes recorded events from claims about hidden model reasoning.
candidates.etymology: Trace comes through French trace for a track or mark; evidence comes from Latin evidentia for what makes something apparent.
known_concerns: A trace is partial instrumentation, not causal proof or faithful access to model cognition; evidence language may grant it too much authority.

candidates.rationale: Names the explicit set of instructions, demonstrations, programs, or artifacts an optimizer may consider. It helps researchers ask which alternatives were representable before interpreting an observed improvement.
candidates.etymology: A technical compound joining search with mathematical space, widely used in optimization and artificial intelligence.
known_concerns: The mathematical noun can suggest a formally defined topology or exhaustive domain when practical candidate generation is heuristic and bounded.

candidates.rationale: Places the metric-to-selection mapping at the center of optimization rather than treating better as self-evident. In a lab meeting the name forces discussion of whose objective is encoded and what behavior it omits.
candidates.etymology: Objective is from Medieval Latin objectivus, relating to an object; function is from Latin functio, performance, and has a formal mathematical sense.
known_concerns: 'Objective' is easily misread as value-neutral truth rather than a chosen function with proxy failures, tradeoffs, and stakeholder assumptions.

candidates.rationale: Names a candidate that is better only relative to nearby alternatives, making the limits of search explicit. It can support skeptical comparison of optimizer trajectories without promising globally best programs.
candidates.etymology: Local comes from Latin locus, place; optimum is the neuter of Latin optimus, best, adopted as a mathematical noun.
known_concerns: Discrete, stochastic program search may not define a meaningful neighborhood, and optimum still sounds like a guarantee rather than an observed candidate score.

candidates.rationale: Suggests retaining program variants that express different tradeoffs instead of collapsing quality, cost, latency, and safety into one score. It gives a paper or benchmark vocabulary for plural optimization goals.
candidates.etymology: Named for economist Vilfredo Pareto; a Pareto frontier contains choices not dominated on all considered objectives.
known_concerns: The name can imply a rigorously computed frontier over complete objectives, while real searches sample few variants and omit hard-to-quantify harms.

candidates.rationale: Describes optimization over textual and structured artifacts where differentiable gradients are unavailable or not exposed. The two-word identity would clearly separate program-level search from model-weight training in technical discussion.
candidates.etymology: Gradient comes from Latin gradiens, stepping, and denotes a vector of derivatives; gradient-free is established optimization terminology.
known_concerns: It narrows the project to an optimizer class, may be read as a performance claim, and does not distinguish random, evolutionary, or model-guided search.

candidates.rationale: Borrows an optimization method that improves one coordinate while holding others fixed, mapping naturally to instructions, demonstrations, and runtime options. It encourages reviewers to ask whether interacting program parts invalidate isolated revisions.
candidates.etymology: Coordinate derives from Latin ordinare, to order, with co-; ascent derives from Latin ascendere, to climb.
known_concerns: The library may use no coordinate-ascent algorithm, and ascent falsely suggests monotonic improvement under noisy or changing metrics.

candidates.rationale: Uses controlled heating and cooling as an optimization metaphor for broad exploration followed by narrower selection. It is compact in code and recognizable in papers through simulated annealing.
candidates.etymology: From Old English onalan, to burn or heat; metallurgy uses annealing for heat treatment, and optimization borrowed it for probabilistic search.
known_concerns: The metaphor may imply an implemented annealing schedule, convergence theory, or material stability that textual optimizer runs do not possess.

candidates.rationale: Names the component that proposes revisions to instructions, demonstrations, schemas, or other artifacts. It makes transformation explicit and allows generation, evaluation, and selection to remain distinct roles.
candidates.etymology: Built from Latin mutare, to change; mutation is used in biology and evolutionary computation for variation operators.
known_concerns: Biological language can naturalize optimization, and the agentive noun may imply autonomous self-modification beyond explicit bounded optimizer calls.

candidates.rationale: Places the credible horizon of generating and selecting structured LM program artifacts beside an established PL research area. The term would invite precise comparison between textual candidate search and synthesis from formal specifications.
candidates.etymology: Synthesis derives from Greek synthesis, composition or putting together; program synthesis is a technical field that constructs programs from specifications or examples.
known_concerns: It falsely suggests formal specifications, correctness guarantees, or broad code synthesis when the current system optimizes declared LM program values and artifacts.

candidates.rationale: Treats optimizer proposals as explicit transformations from one program or artifact to another. The PL vocabulary supports inspectable lineage and makes it possible to ask whether a rule preserves any declared properties.
candidates.etymology: A descriptive technical compound from rewriting systems, where rules replace terms or structures matching a pattern.
known_concerns: LM-generated changes are not necessarily formal rewrite rules and generally do not preserve semantics, types, or observational equivalence.

candidates.rationale: Proposes an intermediate representation for instructions, examples, tool descriptions, and other optimizable artifacts. It aligns with the typed textual horizon while inviting PL researchers to inspect what invariants the representation actually has.
candidates.etymology: IR is the established initialism for intermediate representation in compilers; artifact comes from Latin arte factum, made by skill.
known_concerns: IR implies compiler architecture, stable semantics, and passes over a formal representation that the pre-release library may not define.

candidates.rationale: Maps successive evaluation and transformation stages to compiler passes with explicit ordering and outputs. It could give a future artifact pipeline a clear subsystem identity without requiring one optimizer to own the whole process.
candidates.etymology: Compiler terminology: a pass traverses or transforms a representation, while a pass manager schedules and coordinates such passes.
known_concerns: Compiler wording suggests deterministic transformations and compile-time guarantees; manager wording may also imply a universal orchestration layer.

candidates.rationale: Names a state unchanged by another application of a transformation, offering a rigorous question about when iterative revision stops. It would be memorable in papers discussing optimizer termination and repeated self-critique.
candidates.etymology: A variant spelling of fixed point, a mathematical object x for which a function f satisfies f(x) = x.
known_concerns: It falsely suggests a well-defined deterministic function, proven termination, or convergence; repeated LM revisions can cycle, drift, or vary stochastically.

candidates.rationale: Uses a standard optimization verb for sequences approaching a limit, making an auditable stopping claim central to the name. Its strength is precisely that skeptical audiences can challenge whether observed score plateaus deserve the word.
candidates.etymology: From Late Latin convergere, to incline or turn together; mathematics uses convergence for approach to a defined limit.
known_concerns: This directly overclaims convergence: heuristic artifact search under noisy metrics has no general guarantee of a limit, stability, or improvement.

candidates.rationale: Adopts the DSPy research vocabulary in which optimizers compile one LM program into another program. It is maximally legible in comparison papers and maximally useful for exposing what compilation does and does not mean here.
candidates.etymology: Compiler comes from Latin compilare, to gather together; software engineering narrowed it to translation between program representations.
known_concerns: It can be confused with the Elixir/BEAM compiler and falsely imply static checking, semantics preservation, deterministic output, or official DSPy parity.

candidates.rationale: Combines artifact transformations with an institutional setting for controlled comparison and iteration. It could cover research packages, benchmark reports, and a community without asserting a single optimization algorithm.
candidates.etymology: Transform is from Latin transformare, to change in form; lab is a shortening of laboratory, ultimately Latin laborare, to work.
known_concerns: Lab branding may imply an established institution or scientific validation, while transform is too broad to explain the callable Elixir program boundary.

candidates.rationale: Centers systematic removal or replacement of program parts to estimate which instructions, examples, or modules matter. The engine suffix suggests repeatable machinery for comparative experiments rather than one headline score.
candidates.etymology: Ablation is from Latin ablatio, a taking away; research uses it for experiments that remove components. Engine derives from Latin ingenium, ingenuity or device.
known_concerns: Ablations do not by themselves establish causal contribution when components interact, and engine may imply an automated facility the library does not have.

candidates.rationale: Makes parent-child relationships among candidate programs and artifacts part of the search identity. It supports reproducible comparison by asking not only which variant scored higher but how it was produced.
candidates.etymology: Lineage comes through Old French lignage from Latin linea, line; search comes through Old French cerchier from Late Latin circare, to go around.
known_concerns: Recorded lineage can be incomplete and does not establish causal attribution for gains; the term also risks biological or genealogical baggage.

candidates.rationale: Names the collection of alternatives that an optimizer evaluates, preserving rejected and tied variants as research material. It is deliberately modest and fits data structures, paper methods, and package namespaces.
candidates.etymology: Candidate derives from Latin candidatus, a person clothed in white seeking office; set became a formal mathematical term for a collection.
known_concerns: Set may falsely imply uniqueness and unordered extensional semantics when portfolios preserve duplicate observations, provenance, and generation order.

candidates.rationale: Names the concrete program artifact and evaluation record offered as support for an improvement claim. The witness vocabulary shifts discussion from autonomous intelligence to inspectable before-and-after evidence.
candidates.etymology: Optimization derives from Latin optimus, best; witness comes from Old English witnes, knowledge or testimony, and has technical uses in logic and verification.
known_concerns: Witness can imply a proof object or formal certificate, while a higher observed metric is contingent evidence and may not generalize.

candidates.rationale: Treats conclusions after observing evaluation outcomes as updates rather than final truths. Its statistical familiarity makes it discussable in research, while its compact form works as a library or subsystem name.
candidates.etymology: Latin posterior means later or coming after; Bayesian statistics uses posterior for a distribution after conditioning on evidence.
known_concerns: The library does not generally perform Bayesian inference, and users may infer calibrated posterior distributions where there are only heuristic scores and feedback.

candidates.rationale: Deliberately crosses Bayesian priors, saved ancestor artifacts, and the patent phrase for existing work. It could make inherited demonstrations, baselines, and research provenance visible in both citations and program lineage.
candidates.etymology: Prior is Latin for earlier; prior art is a legal term for publicly available knowledge relevant to patent novelty, while prior has a separate Bayesian technical sense.
known_concerns: The legal collision may suggest patent services, and the Bayesian pun may imply explicit probabilistic priors absent from the implementation.

candidates.rationale: Borrows the language of sets of probability distributions to represent imprecise belief rather than one exact confidence value. The term offers a skeptical audience a compact reminder that uncertainty models may themselves be underdetermined.
candidates.etymology: From Latin credere, to believe; credal sets are sets of probability distributions used in imprecise probability theory.
known_concerns: It is obscure, sounds like credential, and would falsely suggest implemented imprecise-probability semantics or formal belief representation.

candidates.rationale: Names expected loss under a posterior and loss function, foregrounding that decisions depend on both uncertainty and chosen consequences. It would provoke useful criticism of metrics that omit asymmetric costs.
candidates.etymology: Named after Thomas Bayes; Bayes risk is a decision-theoretic expectation of loss under a prior or posterior distribution.
known_concerns: It implies Bayesian decision theory and quantified loss, while ordinary LM metrics may have neither calibrated probabilities nor defensible utility functions.

candidates.rationale: Elevates interval estimates over isolated benchmark points and gives reviewers a familiar handle for repeated evaluation uncertainty. As a category-error brand, it also tests how much statistical specificity the identity can bear.
candidates.etymology: A statistical term developed in frequentist inference; confidence comes from Latin confidentia, while interval comes from Latin intervallum, space between.
known_concerns: The term is frequently misinterpreted and would falsely imply valid frequentist coverage despite adaptive search, dependence, and underspecified sampling.

candidates.rationale: Treats model variance, metric noise, judge disagreement, and dataset shift as costs that must be allocated and reported. It can organize an evaluation report without pretending all uncertainties share one unit.
candidates.etymology: Uncertainty is formed from certain, ultimately Latin certus; budget comes through French bougette, a small bag, later a planned account of resources.
known_concerns: Budget suggests commensurable, known quantities and controllable limits even when epistemic uncertainty cannot be reliably quantified or traded.

candidates.rationale: Makes the strength, source, and limits of a claim part of its presentation. Applied to optimizer reports, it could distinguish measured observations, inferences, assumptions, and unresolved uncertainty.
candidates.etymology: Epistemic derives from Greek episteme, knowledge or understanding; status is Latin for standing or condition.
known_concerns: A label can perform humility without improving evidence, and the phrase has community-specific associations that may feel ideological or self-important.

candidates.rationale: Names failure modes outside the declared metric, dataset, and candidate space. Its awkward plural preserves a hard boundary: optimization can improve observed outcomes without revealing every relevant risk.
candidates.etymology: A plain English phrase with a longer history in risk analysis, widely popularized in public discourse by Donald Rumsfeld in 2002.
known_concerns: The political association is distracting, and the name can become a vague excuse rather than a concrete account of evaluation blind spots.

candidates.rationale: Centers the option for a program or evaluation process to withhold an answer when evidence is inadequate. It gives uncertainty operational consequences without claiming that the LM natively knows when it is wrong.
candidates.etymology: From Latin abstinere, to hold back; statistics and classification use abstention for declining to predict under defined conditions.
known_concerns: The name may imply a reliable reject option or calibrated uncertainty policy that must actually be designed, measured, and enforced by the application.

candidates.rationale: An intentional category error that mechanizes skepticism rather than intelligence. It could name a stress-testing subsystem that generates counterexamples and competing interpretations for declared LM programs.
candidates.etymology: Doubt comes through Old French douter from Latin dubitare, to hesitate; machine derives from Greek mechane, a device or contrivance.
known_concerns: It anthropomorphizes doubt, sounds adversarial for its own sake, and may imply autonomous scientific criticism rather than generated tests requiring human judgment.

candidates.rationale: Adopts the position that claims can remain revisable even when well supported. As a research identity it would frame saved programs and optimizer outputs as provisional artifacts rather than final solutions.
candidates.etymology: From fallible, ultimately Latin fallere, to deceive or fail; fallibilism is associated with philosophers including Charles Sanders Peirce and Karl Popper.
known_concerns: The philosophy label can sound like a doctrine or excuse for defects, and it says little about callable Elixir program mechanics.

candidates.rationale: Signals that metrics, selected artifacts, and research conclusions remain open to revision as datasets and models change. The ordinary scholarly adjective is broad enough for a package and honest about a pre-release system.
candidates.etymology: From Medieval Latin provisio, foresight or provision; provisional means arranged for the present pending later confirmation.
known_concerns: It can undermine confidence in production use and may be read as a temporary project name rather than principled epistemic humility.

candidates.rationale: Names situations where the available evidence supports multiple programs, explanations, or revisions. It is particularly apt for optimization runs with tied scores or metrics too coarse to select among artifacts.
candidates.etymology: A technical compound of under and determine; underdetermination is a philosophy-of-science problem in which evidence does not uniquely settle a theory.
known_concerns: The long negative word is poor spoken branding and may suggest every choice is irresolvable even when practical evidence supports a bounded decision.

candidates.rationale: Describes deliberate variation of prompts, examples, providers, seeds, and evaluation conditions to see whether a conclusion survives. It is a credible subsystem or benchmark label rather than a promise that programs are robust.
candidates.etymology: Robust comes from Latin robustus, strong like oak; check comes through chess vocabulary for a condition that constrains the king.
known_concerns: Passing a finite suite cannot establish general robustness, and the broad term may hide which perturbations and populations were actually tested.

candidates.rationale: Asks how conclusions change when metrics, examples, model settings, or optimizer parameters vary. The established methods phrase is useful for a research toolkit that wants to expose brittle improvement claims.
candidates.etymology: Sensitivity derives from Latin sentire, to feel or perceive; analysis derives from Greek analysis, an unloosening or breaking apart.
known_concerns: The name may imply formal global sensitivity methods or causal analysis when the implementation may only support ad hoc comparative reruns.

candidates.rationale: Turns assumptions about evaluator noise, parsing failures, model variance, and dataset labels into an explicit object of discussion. It would help separate observed failures from a claim about how those failures are generated.
candidates.etymology: Error is from Latin errare, to wander; model comes from Italian modello and Latin modulus, a small measure or pattern.
known_concerns: Most user-defined evaluations do not have an identified generative error model, so the term can imply statistical rigor absent from raw metrics and traces.

candidates.rationale: Names the level below which score differences cannot be distinguished from variability in models, judges, or datasets. It creates a useful challenge to optimizers that report tiny lifts as meaningful.
candidates.etymology: A signal-processing term for the aggregate background noise level below which a signal is difficult to distinguish.
known_concerns: LM evaluation noise is not necessarily stationary or additive, and no universal threshold can separate meaningful change from variance.

candidates.rationale: Names the mismatch between optimization data and future inputs as a first-class limit on program claims. In a critical review, the phrase would demand an account of the reference distribution and observed shift.
candidates.etymology: A modern machine-learning phrase, often abbreviated OOD, for data outside or differing from the distribution represented in training or evaluation.
known_concerns: The phrase presumes a defined distribution that many LM applications lack, and it is cumbersome for package imports and spoken recommendations.

candidates.rationale: Replaces a single answer with a set of outputs intended to cover plausible outcomes under a stated procedure. It creates a bridge to conformal and selective prediction research while retaining an explicit artifact shape.
candidates.etymology: A technical descriptive compound; prediction is from Latin praedicere, to say beforehand, and set is the mathematical term for a collection.
known_concerns: It can imply conformal coverage guarantees or extensional set semantics that arbitrary generated text and user metrics do not provide.

candidates.rationale: A deliberate PL category error that treats uncertain LM output as if it were merely optional typed data. It is useful precisely because a skeptical review can expose the difference between representing absence and modeling epistemic uncertainty.
candidates.etymology: Maybe is ordinary English; monad comes from Greek monas, unit, and in functional programming names a type constructor with specified operations and laws.
known_concerns: It falsely suggests static typing, lawful monadic composition, and a reduction of stochastic semantic error to present-versus-absent values.

candidates.rationale: Invokes Karl Popper's emphasis on conjecture and attempted refutation as a research identity for adversarial evaluation. The proper name would be easy to cite but would place a contested philosophy over a broad engineering library.
candidates.etymology: The surname of Austrian-British philosopher Karl Popper, associated with falsifiability and critical rationalism.
known_concerns: The eponym simplifies a debated account of science, risks personality branding, and does not imply that finite LM evaluations can falsify broad capability claims.

candidates.rationale: Draws on Charles Sanders Peirce's fallibilism, pragmatism, abduction, and community of inquiry. It offers unusually rich research associations for programs revised through evidence and practical consequences.
candidates.etymology: The surname of American philosopher and logician Charles Sanders Peirce, pronounced like 'purse' in his usage.
known_concerns: Spelling and pronunciation are error-prone, the historical figure carries more intellectual scope than the product, and abduction is not autonomous discovery.

candidates.rationale: Uses the canonical name for updating uncertainty in light of evidence. It is immediately discussable among ML researchers and could frame optimization as conditional revision rather than certain improvement.
candidates.etymology: The surname of English minister and mathematician Thomas Bayes, whose posthumously published work underlies Bayes' theorem.
known_concerns: The name falsely suggests Bayesian inference throughout the system, may imply theorem-level rigor, and is heavily overloaded in statistics and software.

candidates.rationale: Links probabilistic modeling, approximation, and a historical vision of scientific prediction to an uncertainty-focused research program. The grandeur of the association makes it a useful adversarial test for epistemic overreach.
candidates.etymology: The surname of French mathematician and astronomer Pierre-Simon Laplace, associated with probability, celestial mechanics, and the Laplace transform.
known_concerns: It is deeply overloaded and can evoke deterministic omniscience, continuous mathematics, or approximation methods absent from the library.

candidates.rationale: Invokes experimental design, likelihood, and statistical testing as a deliberately contentious research identity. It would make assumptions behind evaluation and comparison impossible to ignore in critical discussion.
candidates.etymology: The surname of British statistician and geneticist Ronald A. Fisher, central to twentieth-century statistics and experimental design.
known_concerns: Fisher's eugenics advocacy is a severe historical concern, the surname is generic, and the name would imply statistical methodology not guaranteed by the product.

candidates.rationale: Names a framework for explicit hypotheses, error rates, and decision procedures, giving benchmark gates a formal historical reference. Its hyphenated institutional sound could support a methods project more readily than a package import.
candidates.etymology: Named for statisticians Jerzy Neyman and Egon Pearson, who developed a framework for hypothesis testing using Type I and Type II errors.
known_concerns: It strongly implies a specific frequentist testing regime with controlled error rates, which adaptive LM benchmarks and optimizer selection generally do not satisfy.

candidates.rationale: Invokes exploratory data analysis and the practice of looking carefully before formal confirmation. It suits a library whose traces and reports can support investigation but not automatically turn observations into validated conclusions.
candidates.etymology: The surname of American mathematician and statistician John Tukey, associated with exploratory data analysis, the box plot, and multiple statistical terms.
known_concerns: The eponym borrows a person's authority, is overloaded, and may suggest statistical visualization or methods that are not core product capabilities.

candidates.rationale: Invokes the thesis that tests confront networks of assumptions rather than isolated hypotheses. Applied to LM programs, it highlights that models, adapters, datasets, metrics, and runtime conditions jointly shape a result.
candidates.etymology: Named for French physicist-philosopher Pierre Duhem and American philosopher W. V. O. Quine; the combined label was applied retrospectively to related underdetermination arguments.
known_concerns: The label compresses distinct philosophical positions, is cumbersome in code, and can be used to evade rather than improve experimental diagnosis.

candidates.rationale: Connects a research community to norms of communal knowledge, universal evaluation, disinterested inquiry, and organized skepticism. The lab suffix tests whether those ideals can frame open optimizer artifacts and reproducible reports.
candidates.etymology: Named for sociologist Robert K. Merton, whose account of scientific norms is often summarized as CUDOS; lab abbreviates laboratory.
known_concerns: Mertonian norms are descriptive and contested rather than guarantees, and a commercial or product project cannot claim disinterested institutional authority by naming itself a lab.

candidates.rationale: Uses the Royal Society motto's refusal to rely solely on authority as a compact institution for evidence-bearing LM program research. It could make replication and visible artifacts part of community identity.
candidates.etymology: From the Royal Society motto nullius in verba, commonly translated as 'take nobody's word for it'; nullius is Latin for 'of no one.'
known_concerns: The Latin fragment is opaque and grammatically incomplete alone, borrows institutional prestige, and can perform empiricism without actually supplying reproducible evidence.

candidates.rationale: Frames metrics, calibration practices, benchmark definitions, and reference artifacts as shared measurement infrastructure. The commons architecture would invite collective scrutiny rather than ownership of one supposedly objective score.
candidates.etymology: Metrology derives from Greek metron, measure, and -logia, study; commons refers to resources held or governed for shared use.
known_concerns: Physical metrology's traceable standards do not transfer cleanly to semantic evaluation, and commons implies governance commitments not established by a library.

candidates.rationale: Imagines maintainers and researchers organized around reproducing optimizer claims across models, datasets, and environments. Guild gives visible human stewardship to work often attributed to autonomous systems.
candidates.etymology: Replication is from Latin replicare, to repeat; guild comes from Germanic words for an association organized around shared work or payment.
known_concerns: Guild can imply exclusionary membership or medieval hierarchy, and replication remains difficult under changing proprietary providers.

candidates.rationale: Creates an office-like identity for collecting traces, comparisons, evaluator feedback, and optimizer lineage. Its bureaucratic tone deliberately makes evidence administration visible rather than presenting conclusions as self-authenticating.
candidates.etymology: Evidence is from Latin evidentia; bureau entered English from French for a desk and then an administrative office.
known_concerns: Bureau suggests official authority and paperwork, while collected traces are selective records rather than neutral or complete evidence.

candidates.rationale: Treats component-removal studies as a shared research practice with norms, archives, and disagreement. The grand institutional form is intentionally disproportionate, testing whether critical method can carry a community identity.
candidates.etymology: Ablation is from Latin ablatio, taking away; society is from Latin societas, companionship or association.
known_concerns: The name is comically narrow, society implies an organization that may not exist, and ablation results can be mistaken for causal identification.

candidates.rationale: Invents an institution charged with challenging what optimizer reports, benchmark scores, and generated artifacts warrant. It could support a research process that records dissent and uncertainty alongside selected programs.
candidates.etymology: Epistemic is from Greek episteme, knowledge; review is from Latin revidere, to see again; board developed from a table to a governing body.
known_concerns: It mimics ethics and institutional review authority without governance or mandate, and it can turn epistemic humility into procedural theater.

candidates.rationale: Expands to Declared Artifact Measurement Programs, placing declaration, artifacts, and evaluation in one compact research initialism. The unflattering ordinary word is intentionally retained as an adversarial naming observation.
candidates.etymology: A constructed initialism for 'Declared Artifact Measurement Programs'; damp is also an ordinary English adjective for slightly wet.
known_concerns: The expansion is strained, 'damp' has low-energy negative affect, and measurement programs can sound like surveillance or an objective-metrics platform.

candidates.rationale: Expands to Program Revision by Observed Benchmark Evidence and frames optimization as an investigation. It is concise in imports and gives a paper a method-like name without claiming one universal algorithm.
candidates.etymology: A constructed acronym for 'Program Revision by Observed Benchmark Evidence'; probe comes from Latin probare, to test or prove.
known_concerns: Benchmark evidence may be weak or proxy-bound, and probe carries medical, surveillance, and invasive-testing connotations.

candidates.rationale: Expands to Typed Runtime Artifact Comparison and Evaluation, joining explicit program structures with recorded comparisons. It reads naturally in papers and telemetry discussions while exposing the ambiguity of typed.
candidates.etymology: A constructed acronym for 'Typed Runtime Artifact Comparison and Evaluation'; trace comes from Old French trace, a track or mark.
known_concerns: Typed can falsely imply static type safety, trace can imply complete observability, and the expansion does not distinguish runtime validation from proofs.

candidates.rationale: Expands to Search, Inspect, Fit, Test as a four-stage optimizer and evaluation cycle. The verb emphasizes selection from generated candidates while preserving inspection before adoption.
candidates.etymology: A constructed acronym for 'Search, Inspect, Fit, Test'; sift is an Old English verb for separating material through a sieve.
known_concerns: Fit may suggest statistical fitting or model training, and the tidy sequence hides iteration, leakage, rejected evidence, and human judgment.

candidates.rationale: Expands to Revision Informed by Grounded Outcome Records and directly claims a research virtue. Its overconfident surface is useful for testing whether process vocabulary becomes an unsupported quality warranty.
candidates.etymology: A constructed acronym for 'Revision Informed by Grounded Outcome Records'; rigor is Latin for stiffness and came to mean strictness or exactness.
known_concerns: Naming the system RIGOR falsely certifies methodological quality; recorded outcomes can still be biased, noisy, selectively reported, or measured against invalid objectives.

candidates.rationale: Expands to Program Artifact Comparison Trials and also suggests an explicit agreement about what will be measured. It could frame evaluation configuration as a declared contract rather than an implicit benchmark convention.
candidates.etymology: A constructed acronym for 'Program Artifact Comparison Trials'; pact comes from Latin pactum, an agreement.
known_concerns: The contract connotation can imply enforceable interoperability or stable evaluation standards, and trials may not support causal conclusions.

candidates.rationale: Expands to Evaluation-Conditioned Heuristic Optimization, describing candidate revision driven by returned scores and feedback. Echo also captures repeated calls while leaving open whether repetitions add knowledge.
candidates.etymology: A constructed acronym for 'Evaluation-Conditioned Heuristic Optimization'; Echo is also the nymph of Greek myth condemned to repeat others' words.
known_concerns: The myth can suggest derivative repetition, and evaluation-conditioned optimization may overfit a metric rather than improve the intended behavior.

candidates.rationale: Expands to Witnessed Iterative Transformation, emphasizing saved artifacts and evidence at each revision. The short word works in citations and module names while resisting claims that transformation itself is improvement.
candidates.etymology: A constructed initialism for 'Witnessed Iterative Transformation'; wit is Old English for mind, understanding, or knowledge.
known_concerns: Witnessed may imply formal proof objects or human attestation, while saved traces can be incomplete and do not establish semantics preservation.

candidates.rationale: Expands to Measurable Elixir Text Evaluation and Revision, tying the runtime ecosystem to artifact improvement. The ordinary measurement word makes metrics visible and could support a family of evaluation tools.
candidates.etymology: A constructed acronym for 'Measurable Elixir Text Evaluation and Revision'; meter derives from Greek metron, measure.
known_concerns: It narrows the horizon to text, collides with instrumentation and poetry, and 'measurable' can imply objective or comprehensive metrics.

candidates.rationale: Expands to Named Uncertainty in LM Loops and intentionally collides with the programming sentinel for missing values. It tests whether uncertainty can be made explicit without pretending it is just absence.
candidates.etymology: A constructed initialism for 'Named Uncertainty in LM Loops'; null comes from Latin nullus, none, and is a programming term for no value or reference.
known_concerns: It conflates uncertainty with missingness, has strong failure and database connotations, and LM loops can imply unbounded autonomous operation.

candidates.rationale: Expands to Callable Artifact Laboratory, emphasizing that textual or structured candidates remain executable through declared program boundaries. The laboratory reading gives research scope while the callable term grounds the current API.
candidates.etymology: A constructed initialism for 'Callable Artifact Laboratory'; cal is also an abbreviation for calorie, calendar, California, and calibration in various contexts.
known_concerns: The initialism is extremely ambiguous, laboratory implies institutional validation, and not every optimized artifact is independently callable.

candidates.rationale: Expands to Inspect, Revise, Repeat, a deliberately plain cycle for human-supervised optimizer use. It keeps inspection between generated change and another evaluation rather than narrating automatic self-improvement.
candidates.etymology: A constructed initialism for 'Inspect, Revise, Repeat'; IRR is also a common financial abbreviation for internal rate of return.
known_concerns: The financial collision is strong, the consonant-only surface is awkward to speak, and repeat can imply an endless or autonomous loop.

candidates.rationale: Expands to Language Artifact Bench, combining a test surface with the broader horizon of optimizable text and structured material. It is intentionally generic enough to expose the prestige carried by research-lab naming.
candidates.etymology: A constructed acronym for 'Language Artifact Bench'; lab conventionally abbreviates laboratory, while bench denotes a work or test surface.
known_concerns: The term is generic and crowded, bench can reduce semantic evaluation to apparatus testing, and lab styling may borrow scientific credibility.

candidates.rationale: Expands to Recorded Evaluation for Callable Artifact Programs, emphasizing reports that connect an executable program to measured outcomes. The ordinary verb also suggests reviewing prior evidence before another revision.
candidates.etymology: A constructed acronym for 'Recorded Evaluation for Callable Artifact Programs'; recap is a shortening of recapitulate, from Latin recapitulare, to go over the main points.
known_concerns: The expansion is grammatically forced, recorded evaluation is not necessarily reproducible evidence, and recap may sound like a reporting-only tool.

candidates.rationale: Expands to Hypothesis After Results Known and deliberately adopts the name of a recognized research failure mode. Preserving it as a candidate tests whether an identity can force post hoc storytelling into critical view.
candidates.etymology: HARK is an established acronym for 'Hypothesizing After the Results are Known,' coined in research-methods literature; hark is also an English command meaning listen.
known_concerns: It names questionable research practice, uses a slightly altered expansion here, and could make selective explanation or benchmark overfitting appear endorsed.

candidates.rationale: An intentional overclaim that treats an evaluated LM program as if it were a formally proved mathematical statement. It is retained so PL and ML reviewers can directly articulate the gap between empirical performance and deductive validity.
candidates.etymology: From Greek theorema, something viewed or contemplated; mathematics uses theorem for a proposition established by proof from stated premises.
known_concerns: The name falsely suggests theoremhood, formal premises, deductive proof, and stable truth; benchmark results and runtime validation provide none of those guarantees.

candidates.rationale: Deliberately borrows proof-carrying code for prompts or artifacts accompanied by evaluation records. The mismatch exposes the temptation to promote traces, schemas, and passing examples into formal certificates.
candidates.etymology: Modeled on proof-carrying code, a computer-security approach associated with George Necula in which code carries a machine-checkable proof of safety properties.
known_concerns: Evaluation reports are not machine-checked proofs, prompts are not the whole program, and the name falsely suggests formal safety or correctness guarantees.

candidates.rationale: An intentional category error that maps runtime-validated LM outputs and typed Elixir structs onto thought itself. It gives type researchers an exact target for rejecting anthropomorphism and unsupported static guarantees.
candidates.etymology: Static typing is a programming-language term for checking type constraints without executing the program; thought comes from Old English thoht.
known_concerns: The name falsely implies static type safety, access to model cognition, and type-level guarantees over probabilistic language behavior; the library validates declared structures at runtime.

candidates.rationale: Combines program transformation with the claim that a system can identify why revisions change outcomes. It is retained as an adversarial name for separating comparative experiments from causal inference.
candidates.etymology: Causal derives from Latin causa, reason or cause; compiler derives from Latin compilare and now denotes program translation machinery.
known_concerns: Ablations and score comparisons do not establish causal identification, and compiler falsely suggests semantics-preserving deterministic transformations or compile-time guarantees.

candidates.rationale: An intentionally impossible-sounding category that turns a chosen proxy into a neutral arbiter. Its presence makes the corpus record the strongest form of benchmark reductionism a research identity might accidentally endorse.
candidates.etymology: Objective comes from Medieval Latin objectivus; metric derives from Greek metron, measure, and has formal mathematical and practical evaluation senses.
known_concerns: The name falsely suggests objective metrics free of construct choices, annotation politics, distribution assumptions, and incentives; metric optimization can amplify proxy failure.

candidates.rationale: Pushes optimizer and agent rhetoric to the unsupported claim of independent hypothesis formation, experimentation, and discovery. It belongs in the raw portfolio so critical reviewers can name the human labor and bounded APIs that the phrase erases.
candidates.etymology: Autonomous derives from Greek autonomos, having one's own law; scientist was coined in English in the nineteenth century for a practitioner of science.
known_concerns: It falsely claims autonomous discovery, judgment, and responsibility; the product is a callable Elixir library with explicit tools and bounded optimizer runs, not an independent researcher.

candidates.rationale: Uses the shortest possible ecosystem comparison and therefore tests the exact boundary between philosophical influence and port identity. It would maximize immediate recognition in a citation or package discussion while collapsing important implementation differences.
candidates.etymology: A descriptive comparison to DSPy, the established Python framework name, joined to the Elixir programming-language name.
known_concerns: It falsely suggests an official or drop-in DSPy port, feature and semantic parity, endorsement, and a permanently derivative architecture despite BEAM-native design choices.

candidates.rationale: Combines a specific optimizer lineage with complexity-theory morphology to claim total coverage. The deliberately malformed boast gives DSPy and GEPA researchers a compact example of parity language that should remain contestable.
candidates.etymology: GEPA is the name of an optimizer research lineage; '-complete' is borrowed from complexity classifications such as NP-complete, where it has a precise reduction-based meaning.
known_concerns: It falsely claims parity or completeness relative to GEPA, abuses a formal suffix without reductions or a problem class, and obscures source-fidelity questions.

candidates.rationale: Names a monotonic optimization property that would be attractive in a benchmark headline but is not available for stochastic artifact revision. It forces an explicit distinction between selecting a better observed candidate and guaranteeing future improvement.
candidates.etymology: Guarantee comes through French garantie from a Germanic root for warrant; descent is from Latin descendere, and descent methods move toward lower objective values.
known_concerns: The name falsely promises convergence and monotonic objective improvement despite noisy metrics, adaptive selection, discrete candidates, regressions, and distribution shift.

candidates.rationale: Maximizes category inflation by presenting one pre-release library as the operating system for all research and autonomous improvement. It is intentionally retained as the terminal adversarial observation against platform and agent-OS narratives.
candidates.etymology: Universal derives from Latin universalis, relating to the whole; OS is the standard initialism for operating system, the software layer managing computing resources and programs.
known_concerns: It falsely claims universal scope, durable autonomous-agent orchestration, provider-platform breadth, and institutional authority; the product is an Elixir/OTP library, not an agent OS or provider SDK.
